question: When fats become institutions — laws, sacrifices, gymnasia — which fat belongs to which civilisation?
thesis: Between 1200 and 300 BC oil becomes a civic and sacred substance: Athens measures it, protects its trees and gives it as prizes, while Egypt, Judah and Athena’s temple burn and offer it. Presses and mills make it industrial from Ekron to Greece and India, India builds its ritual and kitchen on ghee, sesame travels from the Indus to Greece and China, and away from the olive cooks still use butter, tail fat and animal fat.

big_ideas.title: In Greece oil is wealth, law and risk
big_ideas.text: Solon allows only oil to be exported from Attica, the archon levies oil from the sacred olives, a wealthy household burns and eats 200–330 kg a year, and a thousand trees make a noteworthy estate. Yet yields swing from year to year, which is why Attic farmers did not specialise in oil.

big_ideas.title: Oil is sacred as well as useful
big_ideas.text: A pharaoh plants olive groves to keep Ra’s lamps burning, Tekoa’s oil goes to the Temple and the Menorah, and Athena’s olives yield the prize oil of the Panathenaic games. The Acropolis olive, burned by the Persians in 480 BC, sprouts again as a sign for the city.

big_ideas.title: Presses and mills make oil industrial
big_ideas.text: Ekron has more than a hundred olive-oil installations in one quarter, Greece the beam press and perhaps the first rotary crusher, and India the ghani, said to be in use from the 700s BC. The machines differ by region and rarely travel.

big_ideas.title: India builds on ghee and mustard
big_ideas.text: Ghee is a prestige fat poured on the sacrificial fire and later used for frying; mustard and safflower become oil sources; and the Buddha allows a sick monk the fat of several animals.

big_ideas.title: Sesame is the oil on the move
big_ideas.text: Sacred in India, pressed in an Urartian workshop, exported in quantity by Darius’s empire, the only oil of Babylon in Herodotus’s account, and a grain in a Macedonian tavern; two Zhejiang tombs push sesame in China earlier than tradition says.

big_ideas.title: Away from the olive, animal fat rules the kitchen
big_ideas.text: Herodotus reports sheep bred for the tail, the Greeks sneer at Thracian butter eaters, and the Zhou court fries a pig in melted fat and cooks each meat in its own seasonal fat.

threads.title: Athens counts and polices its oil
threads.claim: The Attic sources let us count what a household and a city did with oil, and show how the state tried to guard it.

beats.text: Solon allows Attica to export only olive oil of its farm produce, the earliest state measure on oil in the sources, though the Solonian corpus is disputed.
A wealthy household uses 200–330 kg of oil a year, 90–110 kg of it for lighting.
An inscription records over 1,113 amphorae of prize oil at the Great Panathenaia, the crop of some 5,500 sacred trees.
Olive yields swing from harvest to harvest, so Attic farmers do not specialise in oil.
Laconia’s revenues are largely oil, and Plato is said to have financed his journey to Egypt by selling a batch.
The archon levies oil from owners of sacred olives, the law behind Lysias 7.
A thousand olive trees make Hagnias’ estate a noteworthy orchard.

threads.title: Oil for gods, lamps and bodies
threads.claim: In Egypt, Judah and Athens oil is a gift to the gods before it is a commodity, and lamps and washing make it part of daily life.

beats.text: A pharaoh plants olive groves at Heliopolis to keep Ra’s lamps burning.
Tekoa’s oil is sent each year to Jerusalem for the Temple and the Menorah.
Athena’s sacred olives yield the oil given as prizes at the Panathenaic games.
Greek men rub themselves with olive oil and scrape it off with a strigil, in place of soap.
The Persians burn the Acropolis olive, and green shoots spring from the stump.
Clay oil lamps are cheap but their oil is not, so artificial light is a privilege of the wealthy.

threads.title: Crushing and pressing
threads.claim: The first industrial oil works appear in the Near East, and each region develops its own machine.

beats.text: Who brought the olive west, the Greeks or an older Bronze Age tradition, is contested.
Ekron’s industrial quarter holds over a hundred olive-oil installations, the largest known centre of its time.
India’s ghani, a mortar and pestle that crushes and presses in one, is said to be in use from this time.
Greek presses for oil and wine are of the lever-and-weights type, with no screw press.
The 500s BC site at Klazomenai may preserve the earliest rotary olive crusher.

threads.title: India: ghee, mustard and animal fat
threads.claim: Indian fat starts in ritual and moves into the kitchen and the monk’s medicine.

beats.text: Ghee, a ‘commodity of enormous prestige’, is poured on the sacrificial fire.
Mustard seed and safflower are named as oil sources in the Sutras and early Buddhist texts.
The Dharma Sūtras mention vaṭakas fried in ghee.
The Buddha allows a sick monk the fat of the fish, pig, alligator, bear and ass.

threads.title: Sesame’s road from India to Greece and China
threads.claim: A crop that is sacred in India turns up in Zhejiang, Urartu, the Persian empire, Babylon and Macedonia within a few centuries, and each place records it in its own way.

beats.text: Sesame is one of the nine sacred grains, and its oil taila gives a word that later means any vegetable oil.
Sesame seeds lie in two tombs in Zhejiang, 200 to 500 years earlier than the story of Zhang Qian says.
At Karmir Blur an Urartian workshop extracts sesame oil, with pithoi of oil still in the storeroom.
Sesame is exported in quantity under Darius I and the Achaemenids.
Herodotus says the only oil the Babylonians use is sesame, never olive.
Charred sesame seeds lie in a destroyed tavern at Krania in Macedonia.

threads.title: Animal fat at the table: tail fat, butter and the Zhou cook
threads.claim: Away from the olive cooks use animal fat, and the Greeks treat butter as a barbarian’s food.

beats.text: Kiple reports Herodotus on sheep whose tails make up a sixth of the carcass.
The comic poet Anaxandrides calls the Thracians ‘butter eaters’, as an insult.
The Zhou court fries a pig in melted fat and wraps a dog’s liver in its own.
The Zhou Keeper of Victuals cooks each meat in its own seasonal fat.

threads.title: Beyond the Mediterranean: Pacific, Arctic, Africa and Egypt’s castor
threads.claim: Other peoples are already using nut, palm and animal oils, though the evidence is thin.

beats.text: Lapita cooks at Talepakemalai crack Canarium almonds and grate coconut for cream.
The soapstone lamp of the Arctic burns seal and whale oil.
Oil-palm pollen surges in a Niger Delta core, which its author reads as forest clearance for the palm.
Herodotus, Diodorus, Strabo and Pliny report Egyptians burning castor oil in lamps.

turning_points.text: Olive groves are planted to feed the lamps of Ra.
Ghee is poured on the Vedic sacrificial fire.
Ekron builds an olive-oil quarter of over a hundred presses.
Solon limits Attica’s farm exports to olive oil.
Sesame is exported in quantity under Darius.
The Acropolis olive burns and sprouts again.
Herodotus marks the oil frontier: the Babylonians use only sesame.
Foxhall’s household figures show oil as food, light and bath.
Athens levies oil from the sacred olives.
The Zhou court sets a fat for each meat.

text: Sixteen entries, all Greek or western: Athens’s laws, myths and prizes for the sacred olive, a wealthy household’s oil, the beam press and the rotary crusher, the strigil, a Macedonian tavern’s sesame, and the unsettled question of who brought the olive west ([[o1]], [[o2]], [[b3]], [[b4]], [[ec6]], [[ec2]], [[te1]], [[te4]], [[te3]], [[ec5]], [[x1]]). Foxhall warns that Attica did not specialise in oil ([[ec8]]).

Industrial oil at Ekron and sesame at Karmir Blur, Herodotus’s Babylon and his fat-tailed sheep, and the sacred oil of Judah and Egypt ([[ec1]], [[ec4]], [[th1]], [[b5]], [[b6]]). Egypt is filed here by the atlas taxonomy. Egypt’s castor-oil lamps, as the classical writers report them, are here too ([[ec12]]). Herodotus’s fat-tailed sheep, in Kiple, add the animal side ([[th3]]). Darius’s Persia exports sesame in quantity ([[ec15]]).

India: ghee in the Vedic sacrifice, sesame as a sacred grain, mustard and safflower, the Buddha’s fats for the sick, frying in ghee and the ghani ([[b1]], [[b2]], [[ec3]], [[b7]], [[ec10]], [[te5]]); China appears at the Zhou court, cooking each meat in its own fat and frying the pig in melted fat ([[th2]], [[e2]]), and in two Zhejiang tombs of 770–480 BC that hold sesame seeds ([[ec14]]).

One entry: the Niger Delta pollen core, read as oil-palm farming about 850 BC ([[ec11]]). Egypt’s lamp groves and the Nile sit under the Near East. The library has little on sub-Saharan Africa before 1500.
One entry: the soapstone lamp of the Norton and Dorset peoples of the Arctic, burning seal and whale oil ([[te6]]). Nothing else in the library bears on American fats in 1200–300 BC.

One entry: the Lapita village of Talepakemalai, with cracked Canarium almonds, a grated coconut shell and, at Teouma, coconut and nuts in the dental calculus of the dead ([[ec13]]). The Pacific coconut’s spread with the Polynesians is placed in the next folio.

sources.intro: The Greek half rests on one excellent book; the Indian and Chinese halves on a translated reference work each; the Near Eastern industrial sites on a journalist's summary and an atlas folio.
main: Foxhall, *Olive Cultivation in Ancient Greece*, for Athens, the press and the lamp ([[ec2]], [[te1]], [[te2]], [[te3]], [[b3]], [[o1]], [[x1]]).
Achaya, *Indian Food Tradition*, for ghee, sesame and mustard oil ([[b1]], [[b2]], [[ec3]]).
Needham, SCC 6.5, for the Zhou fats ([[th2]]); Bedigian for sesame in Babylon and Urartu ([[th1]], [[ec4]], [[ec5]]).
Mueller and the atlas folio on Philistia for Ekron ([[ec1]]); Khosrova for the butter eaters ([[e1]]).

Foxhall again for the sacred olives, prize oil and the crusher ([[o2]], [[b4]], [[ec6]], [[ec8]], [[ec9]], [[te4]]); Mueller for Tekoa, Ra’s groves and the burned olive ([[b5]], [[b6]], [[b4]]); Achaya and Needham for the ghani and ghee frying ([[ec10]], [[te5]], [[b7]]); Kiple, after Sowunmi, for the Niger Delta ([[ec11]]).
Wikipedia and museum pages found by search for the Arctic lamp ([[te6]]).
Lucas, read from a scanned copy, for Egypt’s castor-oil lamps ([[ec12]]); Legge’s translation of the Record of Rites, in Chang’s anthology, for the Zhou court ([[e2]]).
Kiple (Gade) for the fat-tailed sheep, at second hand from Herodotus ([[th3]]).
Zhao and Mortazavian, in Bedigian’s *Sesame* volume, for Zhejiang sesame and Darius’s exports ([[ec14]], [[ec15]]).
contested: Solon's law ([[o1]]) and the question of who brought the olive west ([[x1]]).
The Athenian household figures are an estimate, not a record ([[ec2]]).
The Zhou li passage was compiled later than the period it describes ([[th2]]).

The date of the Lysias speech is conventional ([[o2]]); the Ra papyrus is dated to Ramses II about 1000 BC by Mueller and usually to Ramses III about 1150 BC ([[b6]]); the Niger Delta pollen is read as clearance, not climate, by one author ([[ec11]]).
The Arctic lamp entry rests on encyclopedia and museum pages ([[te6]]).

The Zhejiang tomb seeds are one report (Chen 1987) that is not seen, and the chapter’s date for the *Qimin yaoshu* conflicts with the sixth-century date used elsewhere in the program ([[ec14]]); the Darius export claim is second-hand ([[ec15]]).
gaps: Phoenician and Carthaginian roles in spreading the olive are only touched ([[x1]]); Egypt under the Ptolemies is in the next folio.
Africa has one entry: nothing here on Nubia, Meroe, Carthage’s own oil or the Sahara, and the library holds little on sub-Saharan Africa before 1500.
Chinese oils are covered only through Needham, India only through Achaya; Central Asia and Southeast Asia have no entry, and the Americas only the Arctic lamp.

how_to_read: Read the thesis and the big ideas first, then the threads: each runs in date order and points to the entries that carry it. Entries that no thread needs are still reached through the regional picture and the lists.

Start with the Greek entries in *Economy* and *Technology*, which are the best-quantified in the folio, then *Belief* for the Indian ghee and sesame. The Nexus links the household oil figures to lamps, the gymnasium and the sacred.
China is the contrast: look at *Thought* for the Zhou fats before the next folio's first pressing of seeds.

The *picture by region* counts the 36 entries: Europe 16, Near East 8, Far East 9, Africa 1, Americas 1, Oceania 1; none in Worldwide. That is the shape of the library, not of the ancient world; the gaps paragraph says what is missing.
